clue.text: Fish with a twist dons blanch okay

indicators.note: the fish dons, or puts on, the blanch word, so it sits inside it like a garment worn

parts.note: to blanch is to turn pale

indicators.note: a twist turns the fish's name round, so it is read backwards

parts.note: the bass is a fish

explanation.surface: A cook's note on a fish dish: blanch it, give it a twist, and it'll be fine.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something adequate, satisfactory without being impressive.

clue.text: Nice inn over in Germany? Time to go round it!

indicators.note: the time word is told to go round 'it', the German word just given, so that word sits inside

parts.note: an age is a long period of time
über is German for over

explanation.surface: A traveller asks whether a hotel abroad is in Germany, and is told to take time to look round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nice' is the French city, not the adjective: the definition asks for an inn in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Auberge is the French word for a country inn or hostelry, as found in Nice.

clue.text: Obvious time to support poor defensive line

indicators.note: in a down answer the supporting piece goes underneath, at the end
poor suggests the letters of the words are in bad shape and need rearranging

explanation.surface: A football pundit says it's obvious: time for something to prop up a poor back four.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges DEFENSIVE with L into SELFEVIDEN; T, placed below it in the down entry, completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something self-evident needs no proof because it is plainly true, which is what obvious means.

clue.text: Cry about nursing year-old males from Wales?

indicators.note: nursing means holding something within, as a baby is held
about means the cry word is turned around

parts.note: to sob is to cry

explanation.surface: Someone weeps over a baby boy, wondering what male Welsh relatives are called.
explanation.definitionFit: Boyo is a Welsh and Irish colloquial term for a boy or man, used as a form of address.

clue.text: Initial sections of cortex or diaphragm

indicators.note: of says the answer is drawn out of the words that follow, running across them

explanation.surface: An anatomy text discussing the first parts of the brain's cortex or the diaphragm.
explanation.definitionFit: An exordium is the opening part of a speech or treatise; this is its Latin plural.

clue.text: Avoid page in How Hollywood Takes Colonics?

indicators.note: in puts the page letter inside the phrase

parts.note: a colonic goes in by the rear, and in American English, Hollywood's, the rear is the ass: 'by ass'

explanation.surface: Steer clear of a page in a lurid book about film stars' colon-cleansing habits.
explanation.walkthrough: The book title is cheeky wordplay: colonic irrigation is taken by the backside, which the American film world calls the ass.
explanation.definitionFit: To bypass something is to go round it rather than through it, i.e. avoid it.

clue.text: They might offer support to people on a flight

definitions.text: They might offer support to people on a flight

parts.words: They might offer support to people on a flight
parts.note: the flight is a flight of stairs, not an aeroplane journey, and the support is a handrail to grip

explanation.surface: Sounds like cabin crew or airline staff helping nervous passengers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests air travel; it is a staircase, and the supports are its handrails.
explanation.definitionFit: Banisters are the handrails beside a staircase that people hold while climbing or descending.

clue.text: Revolutionary drink in China

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning over, so the drink word is reversed in this down entry

parts.note: to lap is to drink as a cat does

explanation.surface: A rebellious beverage served in the People's Republic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country: in Cockney rhyming slang, china plate means mate.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang: china plate rhymes with mate, so china means a friend.

clue.text: A shade obscene? Heavens above!

indicators.note: above puts the heavens word on top in this down entry

parts.note: the heavens are the sky
blue jokes or films are obscene ones

explanation.surface: Someone shocked by a dirty colour exclaims 'Heavens above!'
explanation.definitionFit: Sky blue is a pale, clear tone of blue, one shade among many colours.

clue.text: Comic word-muddler delivering a group of goats?

indicators.note: someone who muddles words, saying the phrase, would come out with something close to it in speech

parts.note: a colony of billy goats would be a 'billy colony'

explanation.surface: A comedian who jumbles his words, describing a herd of goats.
explanation.walkthrough: Say 'billy colony' with the L and N sounds muddled and you get the name. Billy Connolly is a Scottish comedian.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy Connolly is a famous Scottish stand-up comedian and actor.

clue.text: Men embarrassed around small religious groups

parts.note: OR, other ranks, means soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: around means the embarrassed word is turned round

parts.note: an embarrassed person goes red

explanation.surface: Blushing men surround small sects.
explanation.definitionFit: Monastic communities such as the Benedictines or Franciscans are called orders.

clue.text: Old statesman dailies shot hugging royal

indicators.note: hugging means the rearranged letters wrap around the royal letter
shot means wrecked or ruined, so the letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: Newspapers photographed a former politician embracing a member of the royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shot' rearranges DAILIES into DISAELI, which hugs R.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Disraeli was a nineteenth-century British prime minister, a Victorian statesman.

clue.text: Excitement found in exotic tart's charms?

indicators.note: found in says the excitement word sits within the rearranged letters
exotic suggests something foreign and unusual, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: action means excitement, lively activity

explanation.surface: A racy look at the thrill in an exotic prostitute's allure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exotic' gives ATTRS; the excitement goes in before its final S. 'tart' is British slang for a prostitute.
explanation.definitionFit: Charms and attractions are both qualities or features that draw people in.

clue.text: Bolt one Bud? That's reasonable

parts.note: to bolt is to run off, to leg it
I is the Roman numeral one
bud is American slang for a friend, as is mate

explanation.surface: Telling a friend to run for it, then asking if that's fair.
explanation.definitionFit: A legitimate argument or excuse is a valid, justifiable one, as a reasonable one is.

clue.text: Impressed by confession of goalie unable to get off grass?

parts.note: a goalkeeper confessing would begin 'I'm', I am
stuck to the turf, rooted to the spot, is planted

explanation.surface: A keeper admits they can't leave their line, as if rooted to the pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: Together the two pieces make the goalkeeper's admission 'I'm planted': stuck to the spot.
explanation.definitionFit: An idea implanted in the mind is fixed there, as an image impressed on memory is.

clue.text: Row concerning sex in retirement

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the pieces are read backwards

parts.note: re means concerning, about
it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: An argument about sex among the elderly.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is a row or level, as in tiers of seating in a theatre.

clue.text: Hoskins had support cut back on the dole

parts.note: the setter, Hoskins, speaking would say 'I had', contracted to I'd

indicators.note: cut back means the support word loses its end letter

parts.note: a leg supports a table or chair

explanation.surface: The setter laments losing benefit when claiming unemployment.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone on the dole is out of work, so not working, without employment.

clue.text: Over hampered by shocking random bouncer

indicators.note: hampered by means the over letter is held in by the rearranged letters
shocking suggests the letters are badly disordered and need rearranging

parts.note: O is the cricket abbreviation for over, a set of six balls

explanation.surface: A cricket report of a terrible delivery, a random bouncer, spoiling an over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shocking' rearranges RANDOM into DORMAN, which takes O inside. 'bouncer' is a short-pitched cricket ball in the surface, a club's door security in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorman at a nightclub controls entry and ejects troublemakers, as a bouncer does.

clue.text: As herb pie and large bananas?

definitions.text: As herb pie and large bananas?

indicators.note: bananas means crazy, so the letters go wild and are rearranged

explanation.surface: Describing herb pie and big bananas: both foods that go off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bananas' rearranges ASHERBPIE with L. The whole clue also defines: herb pie and bananas spoil quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Perishable food goes off quickly, like fresh herbs and ripe fruit.

clue.text: Race blocking damn time-saving commuter routes?

indicators.note: blocking means the damn word stands round the race word, stopping it

parts.note: rats is an exclamation of annoyance, like damn
to run is to race

explanation.surface: A driver curses as traffic blocks the shortcut on the way to work.
explanation.walkthrough: RAT RUNS is British slang for back streets used by drivers to dodge traffic.
explanation.definitionFit: Rat runs are minor residential streets used as shortcuts by commuters avoiding congested main roads.

clue.text: Where I'm ultra-happy showing up film pioneer

indicators.note: up says the letters are read from the bottom in this down entry, so backwards
showing means the clue words display the answer within them, running across word breaks

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone describes the place of their greatest joy while a cinema pioneer turns up.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft gave 'showing up' to the reversal alone, leaving the hidden step without a signal: 'showing' signals the hidden letters, 'up' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lumière brothers of France were among the first to make and project motion pictures.

clue.text: Shrink to get in touch with grasping Republican

indicators.note: grasping means the touch word holds the Republican letter inside

parts.note: to contact someone is to get in touch with them

explanation.surface: A psychiatrist seeking a greedy right-wing politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' looks like a noun meaning psychiatrist; it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To contract is to become smaller, to shrink, as metal does when it cools.

clue.text: Season fresh tuna without hesitation

indicators.note: without here means outside, so the rearranged letters surround the hesitation sound
fresh suggests a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: um is a sound of hesitation

explanation.surface: A cook seasons fresh tuna straight away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking'; here it means outside. 'fresh' gives AUTN, which wraps round the hesitation.
explanation.definitionFit: Autumn is the season between summer and winter, called fall in America.

clue.text: A rampant do in which husband can't stand

indicators.note: in which says the husband letter is placed inside
rampant means rearing up, so the do word is read upwards in this down entry

parts.note: to do someone is to cheat or rob them

explanation.surface: A rowdy party at which a husband can't bear to be.
explanation.walkthrough: 'do' looks like a party in the surface; it is the verb to cheat.
explanation.definitionFit: To abhor something is to loathe it, finding it intolerable.

clue.text: Where one can see a giant mug sculpture?

definitions.text: Where one can see a giant mug sculpture?

parts.words: Where one can see a giant mug sculpture?
parts.note: mug is slang for face, so huge carved faces, not a huge cup

explanation.surface: Asking where a colossal statue of a drinking vessel is displayed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mug' suggests a cup; it is slang for face, and the giant faces are carved into a cliff.
explanation.definitionFit: The South Dakota memorial has the faces of four US presidents carved into a granite mountainside.

clue.text: Place to study marriage that's not working?

indicators.note: working is on, so not working says remove on

parts.note: a union is a marriage

explanation.surface: A couple whose failing marriage needs somewhere to learn.
explanation.definitionFit: Short for university, an institution of higher education where students study.

clue.text: Coveted post left by head, compete to fill it?

indicators.note: to fill it puts the compete word inside the shortened post word
left by its head means the post word loses its first letter

parts.note: to post a letter is to send it
to vie is to compete

explanation.surface: A job vacated by the boss that people jealously fight to take over.
explanation.definitionFit: To covet something is to want it, as those who envied another's possessions did.

clue.text: Kent society welcomes very southern accents

indicators.note: welcomes means the first pieces take the others inside

parts.note: Kent is a county in the South East of England, abbreviated SE
très is French for very

explanation.surface: A club in Kent receives people with strong southern accents.
explanation.walkthrough: Kent, a county in South East England, gives SE; TRES is French for very.
explanation.definitionFit: Stresses are emphases placed on syllables, which are also called accents.
